name: Delusion (moha)
description: BhG 7–9: the whole world, deluded by the three guṇa-made states, does not recognize the Lord (7.13); the deluded (mūḍha) evil-doers do not take refuge in him (7.15); the deluded world does not know him, veiled by yoga-māyā (7.25); all beings fall into bewilderment at birth through the delusion of the pairs (7.27); the deluded disregard him in human form (9.11) and resort to a deluding nature (9.12).
antidotes: the end of sin, freedom from the pairs (7.28)

name: The pairs of opposites (dvandva)
description: BhG 7.27–28: the delusion of the pairs (dvandva-moha), arising from desire and aversion, into which all beings fall at birth; those of meritorious deeds whose sin has ended are freed from it and worship the Lord.

name: Aversion (dveṣa)
description: BhG 7.27: with desire (icchā), the source of the delusion of the pairs that bewilders all beings at birth.

name: Bondage by the three guṇas
description: BhG 7.13–14: deluded by the three guṇa-made states the world does not know the Lord who is beyond them; his guṇa-made māyā is hard to cross.

name: The demonic endowment
description: BhG 7.15, 9.12: those whose knowledge is carried off by māyā resort to the demonic state and do not take refuge in the Lord; of vain hopes, vain acts, vain knowledge, senseless, they resort to the deluding nature of rākṣasas and asuras.

name: Worship of other gods
description: BhG 7.20–23, 9.23–25, as the text states it: those whose knowledge is carried off by desires resort to other deities, constrained by their nature; the Lord makes their faith firm and it is he who ordains the fruits they obtain, but the fruit is finite — worshippers of the gods go to the gods. Devotees of other deities who sacrifice with faith sacrifice to him, but not according to the rule; not recognizing him in truth as enjoyer and lord of all sacrifices, they fall.
antidotes: recognizing the Lord in truth as enjoyer of all sacrifices (9.24)
notes: The Gītā does not forbid such worship; it calls it finite in fruit and 'not according to the rule'.

name: Lack of faith (aśraddhā)
description: BhG 9.3: those without faith in this dharma do not reach the Lord and return to the path of death and saṃsāra.

name: Desire (kāma)
description: BhG 7.20, 9.21: desires carry off knowledge and lead people to other deities; ritualists 'desiring desires' obtain going and coming. By contrast desire not opposed to dharma is named a manifestation of the Lord (7.11).

name: Attachment to the rewards of ritual (vedavāda)
description: BhG 9.20–21: knowers of the three Vedas who sacrifice for heaven enjoy divine pleasures but return to the mortal world when merit is spent; following the triple dharma with desire they obtain going and coming.
antidotes: knowing the teaching, which passes beyond ritual merit (8.28)
